To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of diaepam and triazolan on repeated acquisition and response sequences with an observation contingency are selective and that the selective effects are not due to the observation contingency.

diazepam and other drugs can selectively increase the percentage of errors during the acquisition of response sequences, and that this selective drug effect can be obtained even though stimulus presentations in the performance component are not contingent upon observing responses.

(a) the selective disruptive effects of diazepam and triazolams on repeated acquisition and the selective non-disruptive effects on repeated performance are not dependent upon observing responding; and (b) these drugs have selective disruptive effects on the repeated acquisition of response sequences that are not maintained by observing responses.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the selective effects of drugs on acquisition and performance are not a simple function of the stimuli presented after a response in the acquisition or performance component.
diazepam and/or triazolam disrupt the acquisition of response sequences by disrupting the acquisition of stimulus control.

the selective drug effects observed in the acquisition and maintenance of response sequences may result from differences between the stimuli that follow each response in these two components of the schedule, and not necessarily from a difference in the nature of the responses emitted in the two components.
